abstract: Dr. Mark Crouch, a US-trained family physician serving in Papua New Guinea, describes the evolution of medical education at Nazarene Hospital. He emphasizes the importance of integrating clinical work with spiritual ministry and adapting training to local realities. Key challenges include balancing overwhelming clinical loads with teaching, and moving from a Western training template to one suited for resource-limited settings. Successes include growing a residency program (Master of Medicine in Rural Health) and seeing a graduate join the faculty. Dr. Crouch advises new missionary educators to first immerse themselves in clinical work and local culture before attempting to lead training.
key_points: Medical education in mission settings must blend clinical competency with spiritual ministry, seeing both as expressions of the gospel.
Western training templates often do not fit resource-limited settings; adapt teaching to available tools and local disease patterns.
Clinical overload can make deliberate teaching difficult; trainees often learn by osmosis in high-volume settings.
Absorbing local culture, language, disease patterns, and faith perspectives is essential before leading educational initiatives.
Successful programs leverage existing national training structures while adding a ministry focus.
Getting promising candidates can be a challenge if the mission hospital's spiritual emphasis deters some applicants.
Having a local graduate join the teaching faculty provides culturally relevant insight and continuity for the program.
Leadership buy-in for training national doctors may take years to develop; momentum builds gradually.
Formalizing training helps ensure ministry and clinical skills are both caught and taught, not left to chance.
Medical educators in cross-cultural settings must be willing to learn from their trainees, who may have valuable local knowledge.
A collaborative, non-authoritarian approach to teaching builds trust and improves the educational experience.
The primary goal of training should not be limited to clinical excellence, which can be achieved elsewhere, but should include navigating the human and spiritual dimensions of patient care.
